chunks: From him, from Hammad, from Abdullah ibn al-Mughira, from Abdullah ibn Sinan, who said:

My father asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) while I was listening to what he said regarding the hubara (a type of wild bird), and he said: 'If it has a falconer (is hunted by falcons), then eat it.' And I asked him about the birds of water, and he said the same. And I asked him about the eggs of the birds of water, and he said: 'That which is like the eggs of the chicken,' meaning in its nature, 'then eat it.'

key_terms.الْحُبَارَى: Hubara, a specific type of wild bird (often bustard) known for being hunted by falcons.
key_terms.قَانِصَةٌ: Having a falconer; referring to birds that are caught by falconry, indicating their permissibility.

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on eating wild birds and their eggs in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies the permissibility of wild game by distinguishing between birds of prey hunted by falcons and waterfowl, establishing a criterion of resemblance to domestic chickens for eggs. This ruling reflects the Shia juristic principle of relying on observable natural characteristics (*khalq*) to determine halal status, bridging the gap between general Quranic permissions and specific dietary laws. The hadith underscores the practical application of *istishab* (presumption of permissibility) in cases where specific textual prohibitions are absent.
